title: Therapeutic Processes in Virtual Reality‐Based Avatar Therapy for Treatment‐Resistant Major Depressive Disorder: A Qualitative Analysis of Patients' Experiences
abstract: ABSTRACT The therapeutic benefits of virtual reality‐based avatar therapy (VRT) compared with conventional psychotherapies remain unknown in individuals with treatment‐resistant major depressive disorder (TRD). Accordingly, this study aimed to explore patients' lived experience of VRT to identify perceived therapeutic processes and benefits, better understand how virtual reality and dialogue with an avatar contribute to therapeutic change and examine how these experiences differed from those associated with conventional psychotherapeutic approaches. A total of 12 individuals with TRD who had completed 8–12 weekly VRT sessions (mean 10.75 sessions) after previously receiving at least two conventional psychotherapies were selected from a clinical trial. Semi‐structured interviews conducted following completion of the VRT were analysed using an inductive qualitative content analysis approach. Six themes describing the therapeutic processes underlying VRT were identified: immersive role‐play, putting theory into practice, the structure of therapy, emotional investment, an atypical therapeutic stance and externalization of internal processes. In addition, three perceived benefits emerged from these processes: integration of therapeutic concepts into daily life, development of mentalization capacities and enhanced self‐determination. Finally, confrontation emerged as a transversal theme linking both the therapeutic processes and their perceived benefits. These findings suggest that VRT combines therapeutic processes common to conventional psychotherapies with distinctive features that may influence how benefits are experienced by patients. Future research should examine whether these distinctive processes account for VRT's added therapeutic value and contribute to clinical improvement.
